0a0b18fc51d7: The Serial Monitor repeats "load:0xffffffff,len:-1" (keeps restarting): under Tools set Flash Mode to DIO, Flash Frequency to 40MHz, Erase All Flash Before Sketch Upload to Enabled, Upload Speed to 115200, then upload again.
0a276f9841fe: Inside the breadboard are metal strips that connect certain holes. Every hole has an address: a row letter (a–j) and a column number (1–30), both printed on your breadboard. So e3 means row e, column 3.
0b5c8e70401a: 330 Ω · orange, orange, black, black, brown. Substitute for 220 Ω if you don't have one.
0e546cc17c80: Getting to know your expansion board
1861081476a6: The red line on the breadboard is for voltage (+), the blue line for GND (−). Never connect the two directly.
24ef0f5b775d: The resistors in the kit can have 4 or 5 color bands. Read from the end where the bands are grouped; the last band, set slightly apart, is the tolerance. If your 10 kΩ resistor is brown, black, orange, gold, it has 4 bands and its value is exactly the same as the one below.
2ccb260840da: Wire color makes no electrical difference. But make a habit of red for +, black or brown for GND, so it is easy to check.
2e10b219186b: A part that used to work stops working: wires on the breadboard are often knocked while fitting a new component. Check that stage again with its test code.
31961cbe5d63: How to put the ESP32 back
3912d5ce3d7a: Compare every wire with the picture and the text in the step. Almost every beginner failure is one wire shifted by one hole.
3a7af0f00046: Upload stops at "Connecting.....": press and hold the BOOT button on the ESP32 until the upload percentage appears, then release.
45d5af972eed: This code has been checked to compile successfully with Arduino ESP32 core 3.3.12, with USE_LCD set to both 0 and 1. The LiquidCrystal library is built into the Arduino IDE; if you get the error "LiquidCrystal.h: No such file", install LiquidCrystal by Arduino from the Library Manager.
4982d11ad349: Two long female sockets, where the ESP32 plugs in.
4f81b0466ee5: The left-hand pin rows for D15, D2, D4, D16, D17, D5, D18, D19, D21, RX, TX, D22, D23. The G/V/S order letters under this column cannot be read in your photo. They are usually mirrored (S at the outer edge), but check the letters underneath yourself before attaching wires on this side.
52620ca961ae: The expansion board's micro-USB and USB-C ports, most likely for power only. To upload code, plug the cable into the port on the ESP32 module itself.
61eb25e00388: The ESP32 suddenly switches off or restarts when plugged in: unplug the USB immediately. Usually a wire connects the red rail straight to the blue one (a short circuit).
7141f61ed77f: The Serial Monitor shows strange letters: change the baud at the bottom right of the Serial Monitor to 115200.
722b5dc73418: This is your own board without the ESP32: the ESP32 ESP32S 30P Expansion board. The numbers in the photo are explained below it.
77838dd75cdc: First get to know every component in your kit, understand how a breadboard works, then build a little at a time. Every stage has a small test code, so you know that part works before moving on.
7892e41d2e5b: Still stuck? Photograph your circuit from above in bright light, send it to me, and say which stage.
792c1fdfff0a: Unplug the USB when attaching wires
7dab9aa09bac: The sensors, LED and Telegram bot you learn here are used again in the 4WD AI Robot: the DHT11 can become the robot's weather sensor directly, and how to read the Serial Monitor and connect wires on the breadboard is exactly the same.
8060c6097f24: The colors on small resistors are sometimes hard to tell apart. A multimeter in Ω mode gives a definite answer. Resistors have no polarity, so they can be fitted either way round.
861fd3085beb: Red: the power rail is connected along its whole line. Any hole along the red line is the same.
86d92d8366df: 10 kΩ (4-band version) · brown, black, orange, gold. Same as 10 kΩ 5-band.
86f303dc5109: The port does not show up in the Arduino IDE: your USB cable may be charge-only, try another cable. If it still does not show up, install the CP210x or CH340 driver (see the text on the small chip near the ESP32's USB port).
8ac103949d0c: The Telegram bot does not reply: make sure the WiFi is 2.4 GHz, the token is correct, the chat ID is correct, and you have pressed Start in the bot.
8b6574011143: Female–female (F-F): pin to pin, for example the LCD straight to the expansion board.
902d47a8f6b3: Your ESP32 is plugged into the black expansion board. Every GPIO pin has one row of 3 pins:
90c9d55a5ec8: The 6.5–16V DC jack for an adapter. Not used yet; USB power is enough.
9524a0c0a2d7: For rechecking a finished circuit (Stages 1–5). "Top" = the rail on the row a side, "bottom" = the rail on the row j side.
995c51b0eba8: The LED does not light: almost certainly reversed. Unplug the USB, turn the LED around, try again. An LED is not damaged by being reversed.
9a74d0961f21: The right-hand pin rows. Each row has 3 pins. The order is printed underneath: G innermost, V in the middle, S outermost (near the edge of the board). The pin names (D25, D26, D34, ...) are printed beside the S pin. The block labeled GND above them holds extra GND pins.
a83486a92b25: The sensors (DHT11, LDR) are given voltage from the red rail, then send a signal to the ESP32 pin at the same voltage. The ESP32 pins are designed for a maximum of 3.3V. Continuously giving them 5V can damage them. If you have a multimeter, after moving the jumper measure the voltage between the V and G pins: the result must be about 3.3V.
a90ace016713: The labels on the expansion board use the format D + GPIO number: GPIO 25 = D25. A full explanation of your board is below.
adb14328a3fe: A total of 6 male-female wires and 6 male-male wires. Count your wires before you start.
aeeda35b13ef: Male = the end is a metal pin (it can go into a breadboard hole). Female = the end is a hole (it fits over a pin).
b4c19e6be4e1: The orientation of the breadboard does not matter. What matters is matching the letters and numbers printed on your breadboard.
b99af48ff90c: S (signal) = the GPIO pin itself, for example D4. The signal wire goes here.
c3231ff6a05b: Unplug the USB first. Face the ESP32's micro-USB port toward the DC jack and the expansion board's USB port (top), with the ESP32's metal can facing down. Match the D15 label on the ESP32 with the D15 row of the expansion board. Make sure all 30 pins go into the sockets with none left outside, then press down evenly and slowly with both thumbs.
c615b2cdc522: Leg under the ⊕ mark in f24
c8eb8fc87c83: The GND, VCC, D21, D22 header for I2C modules, for example the I2C version of the LCD. Not used yet.
cafe3b0e65b4: 220 Ω · red, red, black, black, brown. For the LED.
cc0bb543332b: Orange: f–j in the same column are also connected, but separated from a–e by the gap in the middle.
d496e6c2762b: 100 Ω · brown, black, black, black, brown. For the buzzer.
e2d5f1541e90: Upload fails halfway after the V/G wires were attached: a wire from the V or G pin may be touching (shorting) or drawing excess current. Unplug all wires from the expansion board, upload first, then reattach the wires one at a time.
e33536c10735: Download stasiun_cuaca.ino. Fill in the WiFi name, password, bot token and chat ID at the top of the file before uploading. Do not upload a file that already contains the token to a public place.
e8633a81bd2f: Different columns are not connected. a5 and a6 are not linked.
e9241888dc7e: In every picture, the newly added parts appear bright and the parts from the previous stage appear faded. White dot = a leg or wire end going into a hole. Wires may cross over the breadboard; what matters is that the ends are in the right holes. On a phone, swipe the picture sideways to see the whole breadboard.
f4015f333dfc: All these photos are of your own kit. After reading, turn on guess-the-name mode: each component's name is hidden, try to say it, then tap the card to check.
f4850fe98532: Green: the five holes in one column (a–e) are connected to each other. A component with a leg in a5 is connected to a wire in d5.
f4c22c320f0b: Attach or move wires only while the ESP32 is off. Plug the USB back in after everything is checked.
f64b3c728dfd: 10 kΩ (5-band version) · brown, black, black, red, brown. 2 pieces used.
f8ee2d892e90: Male–female (M-F): expansion board pin to breadboard. The most used in this project.
fa2f6f8969a2: The voltage selector jumper is labeled 3.3V V 5V. Its black cap connects the middle pin (V) to one of the sides, and that is the voltage of all the V pins on the board. In your photo, the cap appears to be in the V–5V position. For this project move it to the 3.3V–V position: pull the cap straight up (use a fingernail or tweezers), then push it onto the two pins on the 3.3V side.
js:ch0: A module with a metal can printed ESP-32, BOOT and EN buttons, and a micro-USB port. In this photo it is plugged into the expansion board.
js:ch1: A black board printed ESP32 ESP32S 30P Expansion board. Every GPIO has a G/V/S pin row, plus a 3.3V/5V selector jumper.
js:ch10: A metal body with a rotating shaft and 3 legs. A marking like B10K means 10 kΩ.
js:ch11: 16 pin holes numbered 1 to 16 along the bottom edge. A pin header must be soldered on first.
js:ch12: A black strip with gold pins. It can be snapped to the number you need (16 for the LCD).
js:ch13: Some are big (12 mm) and some small (6 mm). 4 legs, connected in pairs inside.
js:ch14: A blue board with two cylindrical "eyes". Pins: VCC, Trig, Echo, GND.
js:ch15: A blue box with 3 wires: brown = GND, red = 5V, orange/yellow = signal.
js:ch16: A white plastic piece with holes, plus a small screw.
js:ch17: A blue box printed SRD-05VDC. Pins IN, GND, VCC; screw terminals COM, NO, NC. Do not use it with 220V mains yet.
js:ch2: White board with 400 holes. The red and blue lines at the edge are the power rails.
js:ch3: Three kinds: male-male, male-female, female-female. They can be torn off one by one from the bundle.
js:ch4: Check that the small end fits the ESP32's micro-USB port. (The small item in the middle of the photo is the LDR.)
js:ch5: A small blue cylinder with colour bands. The colours show the value. Not polarised.
js:ch6: Polarised: long leg = + (anode), short leg and the flat side of the body = − (cathode). Always use a resistor.
js:ch7: A black cylinder with a hole on top. The + leg is usually longer, or there is a + mark on the body.
js:ch8: A small disc with a winding line pattern and two long legs. Not polarised.
js:ch9: A blue box with holes and 4 legs: VCC, DATA, (empty), GND.
js:cw0: The brain of the project: runs the code, has WiFi and Bluetooth.
js:cw1: Where the ESP32 plugs in. Makes wiring easier and supplies power.
js:cw10: A resistor whose value is set by turning it. Here it is for the LCD contrast.
js:cw12: A row of pins to solder onto the LCD.
js:cw14: A distance sensor using sound waves, roughly 2–400 cm.
js:cw15: A motor that can be turned to a set angle, 0–180°.
js:cw16: Attached to the servo shaft to move something.
js:cw17: A switch controlled by the ESP32 to turn other devices on.
js:cw2: A board with holes for building circuits without soldering.
js:cw4: Supplies power and uploads code from the laptop to the ESP32.
js:cw6: A small light used as an indicator.
js:cw8: Light sensor: its resistance drops when it is bright.
js:l2: Current flows from D25 → resistor → LED → GND. The resistor limits the current so the LED and the ESP32 pin are not damaged.
js:l3: A passive buzzer contains a small coil that only vibrates when given a fast up-down signal; the frequency decides the note. The 100 Ω resistor limits the current so the ESP32 pin does not work too hard.
js:l4: The LDR and the resistor form a voltage divider. The brighter it is, the smaller the LDR's resistance, the higher the voltage at column 12, and the larger the number the ESP32 reads.
js:l5: The third leg of the DHT11 really is unused. The 10 kΩ resistor from DATA to + is called a pull-up: it keeps the data line stable while the sensor is idle.
js:lcd8: S in the D17 row (on the ESP32: TX2)
js:lcd9: S in the D16 row (on the ESP32: RX2)
js:lcdcap: Pins 1 and 16 are marked with numbers on the edge of the LCD board.
js:o0: The Serial Monitor shows "ESP32 hidup!" every second. If your board has a small built-in blue LED, it blinks.
js:o1: Nothing can be tested at this stage yet. Check again: red is connected to V, blue to G, and no wire goes from red straight to blue.
js:o2: The red LED blinks every half second. Not lighting? Unplug the USB, turn the LED around (swap its legs), try again.
js:o3: Active (the most common, and the buzzer in this kit): part A sounds for a long 1 second, part B sounds as choppy "tek-tek". In the final code leave BUZZER_PASSIVE 0. Passive: part A only clicks, part B gives a clear "tiit". In the final code set BUZZER_PASSIVE 1. No sound at all: check the ⊕ leg and the wire to D26.
js:o4: The number drops when you cover the LDR with a finger and rises when lit with a phone flashlight. Always 0: the wire to D34 or to the red line came loose. Always 4095: the 10 kΩ resistor is not in the blue line.
js:o5: Temperature and humidity appear every 2 seconds with sensible numbers. Blow your breath on the DHT11 (the blue box with holes), not on the LDR: the humidity rises a few percent. "Gagal baca DHT11" all the time: check the leg order and the resistor at a4.
js:o6: The bot replies with temperature, humidity and light. Try /setmax 25: the LED lights, the buzzer sounds, and the bot sends a warning. After that set it back to a sensible number, for example /setmax 31.
js:o7: Two lines of text appear. The screen is lit but blank or shows only boxes: turn the potentiometer, it is the contrast control.
js:p7:
Before this stage

Pin header: the LCD needs 16 soldered pin headers. If your LCD already has a row of pins along its edge, skip this. If not, solder 16 pins (how to solder is in the AI Robot guide, Part 1). A neater alternative: a PCF8574 I2C module for the LCD, so only 4 wires are needed.

5V power: the LCD needs 5V, while the expansion board's V pins are used at 3.3V. The 5V is taken from the power block at the bottom left of the expansion board (the GND column on the left, the column holding the 5V and 3V pins on the right, near the jumper). Plug in the USB, then with a multimeter (V⎓ 20, black probe on a GND pin of that block) find the pin that reads about 4.6-5 V. That is the 5V pin. Unplug the USB again before attaching wires.
js:s0-1: Open Tools → Board → Boards Manager, search for "esp32", install esp32 by Espressif Systems.
js:s0-2: Move the expansion board jumper to the 3.3V–V position (number 1 in the expansion board photo).
js:s0-3: Fit the ESP32 onto the expansion board: the micro-USB port faces the DC jack, the D15 label on the ESP32 lines up with the board's D15 row, and all 30 pins go into the sockets.
js:s0-4: Plug the USB cable into the micro-USB port on the ESP32 module (between the BOOT and EN buttons), not the port on the expansion board.
js:s0-5: Choose Tools → Board → ESP32 Dev Module, then Tools → Port → the port that appears.
js:s0-6: If the ESP32 later keeps restarting (the Serial Monitor full of load:0xffffffff), set: Flash Mode → DIO, Flash Frequency → 40MHz, Erase All Flash Before Sketch Upload → Enabled, Upload Speed → 115200, then upload again. Paste the test code, click Upload (the right-pointing arrow button). If it hangs at "Connecting....", hold the BOOT button until the upload runs.
js:s0-7: Open the Serial Monitor (the magnifying-glass icon at the top right), set it to 115200 baud.
js:s1-0: Make sure the USB is unplugged.
js:s1-1: Male-female wire: the female end to a V pin on the expansion board (any row), the male end to a hole along the red line on the row a side.
js:s1-2: Male-female wire: a G pin → a hole along the blue line on the row a side.
js:s1-3: Male-male wire: from the top blue line to the bottom blue line (the row j side). Now both blue rails are GND.
js:s2-0: LED: the long leg to f16, the short leg to f17.
js:s2-1: 220 Ω resistor: one leg in g16, the other in g20. Bend the legs to fit.
js:s2-2: Male-male wire: j17 → the bottom blue line.
js:s2-3: Male-female wire: the male end to i20, the female end to the S pin in the D25 row.
js:s2-4: Plug in the USB, upload the test code.
js:s3-0: Buzzer: the leg under the ⊕ mark on its top to f24, the other leg to f27.
js:s3-1: 100 Ω resistor (brown–black–black–black–brown): one leg in h22, the other in h24. If you do not have a 100 Ω, use 220 Ω; the sound is quieter.
js:s3-2: Male-male wire: j27 → the bottom blue line.
js:s3-3: Male-female wire: i22 → the S pin in the D26 row.
js:s3-4: Upload the test code. This code also tells an active buzzer from a passive one.
js:s4-0: LDR: its legs to e10 and e12. Either way round.
js:s4-1: Male-male wire: a10 → the top red line.
js:s4-2: 10 kΩ resistor: one leg in a12, the other to the top blue line.
js:s4-3: Male-female wire: c12 → the S pin in the D34 row.
js:s4-4: Upload the test code, open the Serial Monitor.
js:s5-0: Hold the DHT11 with the perforated side facing you. Push its 4 legs into e3 e4 e5 e6 (the leftmost leg in e3).
js:s5-1: Male-male wire: a3 → the top red line.
js:s5-2: Male-male wire: a6 → the top blue line.
js:s5-3: 10 kΩ resistor: one leg in a4, the other to the top red line.
js:s5-4: Male-female wire: c4 → the S pin in the D4 row.
js:s5-5: In the Arduino IDE: Tools → Manage Libraries, install the DHT sensor library (Adafruit). Choose "Install all" when asked.
js:s5-6: Upload the test code, open the Serial Monitor.
js:s6-1: In Telegram, chat with @BotFather, send /newbot, follow the instructions, and save its token.
js:s6-2: Chat with @userinfobot, and save your Id number.
js:s6-3: Open your new bot and press Start.
js:s6-4: Open the file stasiun_cuaca.ino, fill in the WiFi name, password, token and chat ID. Make sure USE_LCD is 0 (it already is by default), and BUZZER_PASSIVE matches the result of Stage 3. The WiFi name must be a 2.4 GHz network; the ESP32 cannot do 5 GHz. Fill it in with your own home WiFi, not a made-up name. Enter the token and password only on your own computer; do not upload them to GitHub or share them.
js:s6-5: Upload. The bot will send "Stasiun cuaca menyala". Send /status. Once it works, the ESP32 no longer needs the IDE: just plug it into a 5V USB adapter and it runs by itself.
js:s7-0: Potentiometer: its 3 legs to f3 f5 f7.
js:s7-1: Male-male wire: j3 → the bottom red line. Male-male wire: j7 → the bottom blue line.
js:s7-2: Male-female wire: the 5V pin of the power block (the one you found earlier) → the bottom red line. Never connect the bottom red line to the top red line (3.3V).
js:s7-4: Connect the other LCD pins following the table below.
js:s7-5: Upload the LCD test code, then turn the potentiometer slowly until the text is visible.
js:s7-6: In the final code, set USE_LCD to 1 and upload again.
js:t0: Set up the laptop and test the ESP32
js:t6: Final code and the Telegram bot
